provenance: Opus 5.5 subscription CLI draft with host review/repairs, source restrictions and execution verification.

draft_notes.explanation: Same mechanism as the constructor. The background is the most common colour. The divider is the colour of the largest non-background 4-connected single-colour object. Regions are the 4-connected components of non-divider cells. For each region, every seed is walked along each of the four diagonals to the end of the region. That end must be a convex corner for the diagonal: both orthogonal outward neighbours lie outside the region. The reading goes from that corner inward and is truncated after its last coloured cell. The program picks the reading with the most coloured cells. Each region cell is painted chain[(ring-1) % len], where ring is the Chebyshev distance to the complement. The only change from the failed candidate is the tie-break among readings with equal coloured counts. It used to be whichever reading appeared first in iteration order, which depends on orientation. Now it is fewest leading background cells, then shortest reading. That selects the reading anchored nearest its corner, which matches how the generator places chains: flush to a corner, with at most one leading background cell. This key does not depend on scan order, so it gives the same choice under every D4 map and palette.
draft_notes.limitations: If two corner readings in one region match on coloured count, leading-background count and length but differ in content, the choice falls back to reading-order iteration. The constructor's _chain_ok rejects such scenes for random generation. None of the canonical fixtures appears to contain one, but I checked that by hand reasoning, not by running anything. Divider detection assumes the divider forms the largest non-background single-colour component, which the constructor's colour-count and layout constraints imply. No tests were run.
draft_notes.diagnosis: The counterexample is d4=1 with the identity palette, and the failing check (index 2) is train pair 3. After rotation, the region that should become all 7 is a 6x6 square: rows 7-12, cols 4-9. Its only seed, 7, sits at corner (12,9), and the diagonal through it runs corner to corner, ending at another convex corner, (7,4). That gives two corner-anchored readings with one coloured cell each: [7] from (12,9), and [8,8,8,8,8,7] from (7,4). The failed solver breaks ties by taking the first reading found. In the rotated grid it tries direction (-1,-1) first and gets [8,8,8,8,8,7], whose ring colours for a 6x6 region (rings 1-3) are all 8. So the region stays background instead of turning 7. In the unrotated orientation, iteration order happens to find [7] first, which is why the archived solver passes the canonical fixture. The fix is a scan-order-free tie-break: prefer fewer leading background cells, then the shorter reading. This is not a special case. It encodes the generator's placement rule that the chain starts at its corner with at most one leading background cell.
draft_notes.constructor_issue: The canonical fixture train pair 3 (explicit chain (0,12,1,-1,[7]) in a 6x6 square region) is ambiguous under the constructor's own uniqueness criterion. Its _chain_ok would see the readings {(7,), (8,8,8,8,8,7)} and reject the scene. validate() builds canonical pairs from explicit chains and skips _chain_ok, so the ambiguity is never caught. The label itself matches the intended mechanism (the chain is anchored at the corner where it was placed), and labels were not modified. Solvers that rely only on max-coloured-count with order-dependent tie-breaking will fail on some D4 variants of this fixture.
